19913-omaha-dwellings-furniture-and-impl:
Alice Fletcher and Francis La Flesche documented Omaha life for the Bureau of Ethnology. This study of dwellings, furniture, and implements appeared in the Thirteenth Annual Report. The Omaha's primitive homes were chiefly earth lodges. Bark or mat lodges came second in their account. Skin lodges, or tipis, served for travel and hunting. No sacred rites attached to lodge-building among the Omaha and Ponka, they note.

La Flesche, himself Omaha, gave the work insider knowledge. Fletcher's measurements and plans set an ethnographic standard. Houses encode kinship, season, and ceremony in their forms. The report preserves building knowledge elders still held then. It remains a foundation source on Omaha material culture.
20456-notes-on-certain-maya-and-mexican-:
Notes on Certain Maya and Mexican Manuscripts is a scholarly paper from the Third Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology. It studies the picture writings left by the Maya and the peoples of Mexico. Scholars of the time were just learning to read these old books.

The writer had lately obtained Léon de Rosny's work on the written documents of ancient America. It held a photo-lithographic copy of two plates, or rather one plate in two parts. Comparing such copies was the only way to study codices kept in distant libraries. The paper shows early American archaeology at work.
21725-the-coxswain-s-bride-also-jack-fro:
Three tales by R. M. Ballantyne sit together in this volume, and the first follows lifeboat coxswain Robert Massey. Sturdy Bob, his mates call him, and handsome Bob to the women of his village. He leads the Greyton lifeboat, and his bride-to-be, a fair-haired fisher girl, waits ashore. Their smooth courtship opens the story on a calm, bright evening.

Storm and wreck soon test the coxswain and his crew, as lifeboat tales must. The two shorter tales that follow, Jack Frost and Sons and A Double Rescue, keep to Ballantyne's home ground of sea, weather, and brave deeds. Together they show his range in short form: love, duty, and rescue on a hard coast.
22457-the-verbalist-a-manual-devoted-to-:
Alfred Ayres wrote The Verbalist, a manual on speaking and writing with propriety. Its subtitle promises brief discussions of rules for good usage. Ayres corrects errors of grammar, wording, and pronunciation throughout.

His authorities fill a shelf of nineteenth-century language books. Bain's and Quackenbos's composition grammars stand among his sources. Cobbett's and Goold Brown's English grammars also guide him. Graham's and Crabb's books of synonyms settle fine word choices. Bigelow's Handbook of Punctuation handles stops and marks. The Verbalist distills all that learning into short, firm rulings. It preserves an age when correct English felt like a moral duty to many.
a-smaller-history-of-greece-from-the-ear:
William Smith compresses Greek history for students, from the geography of the land and the heroic age to the Roman conquest. His contents move in clear order: the rise of Sparta and Athens, the Greek colonies, then the Persian Wars from the Ionic revolt through Marathon, Thermopylae, Salamis, and Plataea.

Chapters on Athens under Pericles and the three periods of the Peloponnesian War follow, then the Thirty Tyrants, the death of Socrates, Macedon's rise, and the age after Alexander. Smith, a famous classical editor, writes plainly and keeps dates and causes in view. Generations of school readers learned their Greece from this compact, orderly survey.
capek-r-u-r:
Capek wrote R.U.R. in Czech, and Czech readers meet the play here in its first tongue. Artificial workers pour from Rossum's factory to serve mankind. Made only for labor, they gain grievances, leaders, and at last the will to rebel.

The drama, first staged in 1920, coined the word robot for all the world. Beneath the marvel runs a hard question about work and worth. Capek gives even his rebels a claim on pity. In its own language, the play shows its wit and rhythm best, a landmark of Czech letters and of modern drama.
charles-philip-yorke-fourth-earl-of-hard:
Lady Biddulph's memoir of her father, Charles Philip Yorke, Fourth Earl of Hardwicke, Vice-Admiral, draws on the letters and journals he left to her care. Biddulph, his daughter, writes with diffidence, since this is her first experience of such work, but her reasons seem to her unanswerable.

Her father's active, varied life, and the large part he played in his day's affairs, deserve a fuller account than reference works supply. Biddulph presents in outline a capable, energetic Englishman, loyal and devoted to sovereign and country. Readers of naval and Victorian biography will find the memoir a labour of love, rich in letters and journals.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GiesbrechtRicha:
Five writers joined in an investigative article about Richard Giesbrecht, an insurance salesman from Winnipeg. In February 1964, Giesbrecht gave the FBI evidence of a multi-man plot to kill President Kennedy. Later, he said, agent Merle Nelson told him to forget what he had brought them.

A witness with evidence of a plot, told to forget it, is the heart of many assassination controversies. The article examines Giesbrecht's treatment at the Bureau's hands and the evidence he carried. It preserves a Canadian side door into the case, reported by a team of five journalists.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NaimanJasonR_Na: Harold Weisberg, in all likelihood, wrote this letter, dated January 15, 1970, to Jason R. Neiman. govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WroneDavidR_Wro:
David R. Wrone, a historian at the University of Wisconsin, spent years listing nearly everything written about the Kennedy assassination. His annotated bibliography holds 2,376 entries on the killing of John Fitzgerald Kennedy, and each entry carries a note from the author.

A bibliography with notes does more than list titles. Wrone tells the reader what each item is, who wrote it, and why it matters, across books, magazine articles, pamphlets, and official reports. For anyone entering the huge literature on the assassination, his volume works as a map drawn by a scholar who read the territory himself and marked the sound ground.
govdocs-archive_org-spiritual-authority-:
René Guénon published Spiritual Authority and Temporal Power in 1929, a short book with a firm claim. It states the Traditionalist doctrine of the two powers: priesthood above kingship, spiritual authority above temporal rule.

Guénon argues that healthy societies keep that order, with kings guarding a law they do not invent and priests guarding the truth that law serves. When rulers claim the highest place for themselves, he says, decline and confusion follow in every part of life. The book is central to his work. Readers meeting Guénon for the first time often start here, because his whole system appears in it in compact form.
lessons-of-the-war-being-comments-from-w:
Spenser Wilkinson published his weekly war comments as Lessons of the War in 1900. Archibald Constable issued the book in London and Philadelphia. Chapters begin with the eve of the South African war.

Titles trace a week's campaign, playing with fire, and Buller's problem. Wilkinson asks how weak policy leads to bad strategy. He presses for reinforcements and calls the war the nation's business. His comments ran while the Boer War still unfolded. Readers get a military critic thinking in public, week by week. A chapter asks simply for the right man to lead. Wilkinson later became a noted military historian at Oxford.
nasa-tm-19660001934-a-system-for-automat:
Neal E Reid at Goddard described a system that gathers radiation test data on its own, in this August 1965 report. Semiconductor devices, the parts of modern circuits, change under radiation. Testing them means logging many readings over long exposures. Reid's system uses a digital clock, a scanner, and a relay box to collect those readings automatically.

Automatic logging removes hours of hand recording. It also cuts the errors that creep into hand-copied tables. Radiation data decided which electronic parts could fly. A system that gathered the data steadily, day and night, made those judgments faster and firmer for the engineers who relied on them.
nasa-tm-19660015402-on-the-production-of:
P B Abraham, K A Brunstein, and T L Cline at Goddard asked where low-energy cosmic ray electrons come from, in this February 1966 paper. Cosmic ray electrons arrive from space at many energies. The low-energy ones are the hardest to trace, because the solar wind bends their paths and changes their energies on the way in. Their origins could lie in the Sun, or far beyond it.

Sorting those origins shapes models of how particles fill the solar system. The paper belongs to Goddard's energetic particles preprint series. Such electrons also affect the radiation setting near Earth. A clear account of their production helps both pure science and the practical work of shielding crews and instruments.
nasa-tm-19670019840-description-and-desi:
Loren W. Acker, Nick J. Sekas, and Seymour Lieblein, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, describe a test facility in this memorandum. The facility serves liquid-metal radiators and condensers, hardware that dumps waste heat from space power systems. Liquid metals carry heat well, but they must be tested on the ground first.

The contents show the facility's layout in detail. Separate loops handle heating, vapor, and cooling duties. Component sections cover piping, material selection, stress calculations, and pressure losses. A primary heater gets its own treatment. The document is a design record for engineers building or using such rigs.
nasa-tm-19710018260-the-effects-of-charg:
Walter A. Wappaus conducted this test series on spacecraft mirror coatings that control temperature by reflecting sunlight. The coatings were silvered and aluminized FEP Teflon films used as second surface mirrors. In orbit such coatings face electrons, protons, and ultraviolet light, all of which can darken them and spoil their cooling power.

Wappaus irradiated both coatings with electrons and protons at two energy levels and with ultraviolet light as strong as five suns. He also tested ultraviolet and charged particles together, as real space delivers them. The results show both coatings suffer more from higher-energy protons than from electrons of the same energy. Combined exposure hurt more than particles alone at high doses, while ultraviolet alone in vacuum left the coatings virtually unchanged.
nasa-tm-19710022892-skylab-three-axis-mo:
Michael T. Borelli of the Marshall Space Flight Center and Jack Templeton of Sperry Rand Corporation reported these results in June 1971. Their report was issued as NASA TM X-64609. Their subject was STAMP, the Skylab three-axis motion platform. The platform tilts and turns a load in three axes to mimic spacecraft motion for tests and training.

The report describes the system, states its performance requirements, and then walks through the test program section by section. Tests covered frequency response, transient response, position and rate accuracy, stiffness, and gimbal friction. A parameter sensitivity test and a discussion with recommendations close the main text. Illustrations show control moment gyros mounted in torque measuring fixtures on the load platform, the hardware the platform was built to exercise.

the-bible-douay-rheims-book-53-1-corinth:
First Corinthians, in the version of Douay-Rheims, an English rendering of the Latin Vulgate revised by Bishop Richard Challoner over 1749 to 1752. Its two parts first appeared at Rheims in 1582 and at Douay in 1609 and 1610. An introduction says Paul treats several matters of faith, morals, and church discipline in the letter.

Chapter one rebukes divisions about teachers. The world, Paul argues, was to be saved by preaching of the cross, not by human wisdom or fine speech. Paul writes as a called apostle, with Sosthenes, to a church in Corinth. Quarrels over leaders give the letter its start. From that local split, Paul moves to questions that still shape church teaching.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-54-2-corinth:
Second Corinthians, in Douay-Rheims English drawn from the Latin Vulgate, in the revision Bishop Richard Challoner finished across 1749 to 1752. Rheims in 1582 supplied the New Testament, Douay in 1609 and 1610 the Old Testament. An introduction says Paul recounts his sufferings and the graces God gave him. The letter was written in the same year as the first and sent by Titus from Macedonia.

Chapter one speaks of Paul's troubles in Asia. His failure to come was not levity, he insists, and his doctrine is constant and sincere. Paul writes with Timothy to the church at Corinth and all the saints nearby. Defence of his own ministry, unusual in a letter, fills much of what follows.
the-fourth-r:
George O. Smith wrote The Fourth R as a novel of a boy raised to a fierce pitch of learning, under a copyright of 1959. James Quincy Holden is five years old on the first page.

Jimmy's fifth birthday starts at seven with cocktails for the grown-ups, while he sips ginger ale. His gifts run to Kipling's Jungle Tales, a small planetarium, and a kit for building a Geiger counter with real samples to test. He picks the dinner menu and the music, then wins at bridge. Smith builds a tale of what a brilliant child, pushed by grown schemes, might do to the world that made him.
the-gutenberg-webster-s-unabridged-dicti:
Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary, in the version published in 1913 by the C. & G. Merriam Co. of Springfield, Mass., under the direction of Noah Porter, covers English words in alphabetical order. The portion here holds the letter R. It begins with a note on the letter itself, calling it a vocal consonant and a liquid, and tracing its form through Greek and Latin.

Word entries follow, each with pronunciation, origin, and sense. Early entries include Ra, the prefix Ra-, Raash for the electric catfish, Rab, and Rabat. The section also explains the phrase the three Rs for reading, writing, and arithmetic. Notes mark old or local uses and cite writers as support.
tom-swift-and-his-motor-cycle-or-fun-and:
Victor Appleton's first Tom Swift book opens on a country road, where two lads in a touring car urge red-haired Andy to shove the spark lever and make a record. Contents promise twenty-five chapters of fun and adventures on the road, starting with a narrow escape. Tom overhears something, suffers a smash-up, and gets his motor-cycle.

Later headings bring a vindictive tramp, men in an auto, a storm, a strange mansion, pursuit, and unexpected help. Mr. Swift despairs midway, and a man called Eradicate saws wood and gives a clue. Readers get the series launch, with speed and suspicion from the first page.
